claims.claim: Adolescence is the phase of life between childhood and adulthood, from about ages 10 to 19 (WHO working definition); other sources draw the borders differently (OpenStax Psychology 2e frames the age range as 12 to 18).
Adolescence entails rapid physical, cognitive, and psychosocial growth — the transitions that carry an individual from childhood to adulthood.
Adolescence begins with puberty; the sequence of physical changes is predictable, but the onset and pace vary widely between individuals.

The adolescent brain is still developing: the prefrontal cortex — responsible for planning, prioritizing, and decision making — is one of the last regions to mature, and the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late twenties.

During adolescence the frontal lobe and its connections to the limbic system are still maturing, which can be associated with occasional difficulty with inhibition, emotional regulation, and attention.
The teen brain is ready to learn and adapt, and it is resilient.

Piaget's formal operations — the final stage of his cognitive development theory, reached in adolescence — bring the ability to reason with formal logical systems and symbols, including abstract and hypothetical possibilities; younger children reason well but are limited to concrete situations.

Peers gain importance in adolescence: it is a time of heightened sociability, often beyond direct adult supervision, and peer relationships act as a transitional force as adolescents turn outward from the family toward the wider society.
Erikson's fifth psychosocial stage — identity versus role confusion, roughly ages 12 to 18 — frames identity formation as the central task of adolescence.

G. Stanley Hall famously characterized adolescence as a period of 'storm and stress', but the research evidence indicates most teens do not experience turmoil to that degree; only small numbers of teens have major conflicts with their parents, and most disagreements are minor and concern everyday issues.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Storm and stress: is adolescence inherently a time of turmoil?
positions: G. Stanley Hall's famous characterization of adolescence as 'storm and stress'
Research reviewed by OpenStax: most teens do not experience storm and stress to that degree; most parent-teen conflicts are minor
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Hall's idea as a historical framing and the research finding as the evidence-based reality check, with no alarm language.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reading of the brain note: 'developing into the mid-to-late twenties' can be misread as 'teenagers cannot make decisions'
positions: Brain maturation continues into the mid-to-late twenties (NIMH)
The same source stresses the teen brain is ready to learn and adapt and is resilient
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the maturation fact plainly and pairs it with NIMH's learn-and-adapt and resilience framing, avoiding both scare content and over-claiming incapacity.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 9.1: Physical Growth and Development in Adolescence
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via Internet Archive Wayback capture 20260211063529 of the canonical URL. Supports: adolescence as entailing the physical, cognitive, social, and emotional transitions of an individual from childhood to adulthood; the frontal lobe and prefrontal cortex as the center of executive functioning; the limbic system developing alongside; frontal-lobe-to-limbic connections still maturing during adolescence, associated with occasional difficulties in inhibition, emotional regulation, and attention; wide individual variability in physical growth. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 9.3: Cognition in Adolescence
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via an Internet Archive Wayback capture (2025) of the canonical URL. Supports: Piaget's formal operational stage as the final stage reached in adolescence — reasoning with formal logical systems and symbols; the ability to think about all the possibilities in a situation and test them; hypothetical reasoning about situations that do not exist; younger children reasoning well but limited to concrete, physical situations; Piaget's view that cognitive development is complete during adolescence. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 10.1: Theories of Adolescent Socioemotional Development
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via an Internet Archive Wayback capture (2025) of the canonical URL. Supports: Erikson's fifth psychosocial stage, identity versus role confusion, typically ages twelve to eighteen; forming a coherent identity takes time and adolescence accommodates this key developmental task; identity described as adolescence's central challenge. Used for a one-line pointer only — the identity topic owns the detail. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 10.4: Social Contexts in Adolescence
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via an Internet Archive Wayback capture (2025) of the canonical URL. Supports: adolescence as a time of heightened sociability, often beyond the direct supervision of parents or other adults; the gradual turning outward from the family toward society at large (Havighurst, cited therein); peers and peer relations as a transitional force; brain development supporting heightened interest in peers and other social cues; friendships becoming more stable and enduring as adolescence progresses. Facts synthesized in original prose.
